div.l: ¶ Here beginneth the Prolog of the tales of Caunterbury
Whan that Aprill with his showres swote
The drought of Marche hath ꝑperced þe rote
And bathed euer in wyn in suche licoure
Of which vertu engendereth is the floure
Whan zepherus eke with his swote brethe
Enspired hath in eueri holt and hethe
The tendre croppes and the yong sonne
Hath in the Ramme his half cours y ronne
And smale foules maken melodye
That slepen all night with open ye
So priken hem nature in here corage
Than longen folk to go on pilgrimage
And palmers to chesen strange strondes
And halowes couth in many londes
And specialli from eueri shires ende
Of Ingelond to Caunterbury thei wende
To seche the blisfull marter that is meke
That hem hath holpen whan þei were seke
It befell þat in þat cesoıı̄un on a day
In South werk atte Tabard as I lay
Redi to wende on my pilgrimage
To Caunterbury with deuoute corage
And night was comyn̄ in that herbary
Well xxix in a company
Of sondri folk be auenture I fall
In felashipp as pilgrymes were thei all
That touard Caunterbury wold ride
The chambres and hall were wide
And well were þei esed atte best
And shorteli whan the son was gon to rest
So had I spoken with hem euerich oon̄
That I was of here felaship a noon̄
And made foreward erli for to rise
To make oure wei ther as I yow devise
But nathalese while I haue tyme and space
Or that I forther in this tale pase
Me thenk it according to resoun̄
To tell you al þe condicioıı̄un
Of eche oon̄ of hem so as it semed me
And which þei were / and of what degre
And in what a rai þei were yn̄
And atte a knight I will begyn̄
knight þere was and þat a worthi man̄
